s0101.literal: At that time Liu Yi held Dongyang in his grip, privately appointing prefectural and county officials; the Founder was troubled by it and therefore made Zhaoda magistrate of Changshan county, placing him in Yi's heartland.
s0101.idiomatic: At that time Liu Yi held Dongyang, appointing his own officials; the Founder, troubled by this, made Zhaoda magistrate of Changshan county to plant him in Yi's heartland.

s0102.literal: In the second year of Yongding he was made magistrate of Wukang.
s0102.idiomatic: In Yongding year two he was made magistrate of Wukang.

s0103.literal: When Emperor Wen succeeded to the throne, [Zhaoda] was made supernumerary scattered-cavalry regular attendant.
s0103.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen succeeded, Zhaoda was made supernumerary scattered-cavalry regular attendant.

s0104.literal: In the first year of Tianjia, for merit at the defense of Changcheng he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xinle county, fief of one thousand households.
s0104.idiomatic: In Tianjia year one, for merit at Changcheng he was enfeoffed as marquis of Xinle county with a fief of one thousand households.

s0105.literal: Soon he followed Hou Andu and others in resisting Wang Lin at
s0105.idiomatic: Soon he followed Hou Andu and others in resisting Wang Lin at

s0107.literal: [Zha]kou; Editorial footnote marker 5. they fought at Wuhu; Zhaoda rode the Flat-Barbarian great ship, advanced midstream, and the vanguard's pounders struck the rebel ships.
s0107.idiomatic: [Zha]kou. [5] At Wuhu, Zhaoda sailed the Flat-Barbarian great ship midstream; the vanguard's pounders struck the rebel ships.

s0108.literal: When Wang Lin was pacified, Zhaoda's registered merit ranked first.
s0108.idiomatic: When Wang Lin was suppressed, Zhaoda's merit was entered first on the rolls.

s0109.literal: In the second year he was made bearer of the staff, scattered-cavalry regular attendant, area commander over military affairs in the four prefectures of E, Ba, Wu, and Yuan, intelligent-martial general, and inspector of E prefecture; his fief was increased to one thousand five hundred households in all.
s0109.idiomatic: In year two he was made bearer of the staff, scattered-cavalry regular attendant, commander of armies in E, Ba, Wu, and Yuan prefectures, intelligent-martial general, and inspector of E prefecture, with his fief raised to one thousand five hundred households in all.

s0110.literal: Soon he was advanced in title to general who pacifies the west.
s0110.idiomatic: He was soon promoted to general who pacifies the west.

s0111.literal: Zhou Di held Linchuan in rebellion; an edict ordered Zhaoda to campaign against him by convenient route.
s0111.idiomatic: Zhou Di rebelled in Linchuan; an edict sent Zhaoda against him by the direct route.

s0112.literal: When Di was defeated and fled, [Zhaoda] was summoned as protector general and granted a troupe of martial music; he was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Shaowu county, his fief increased to two thousand households in all; his regular attendant status was unchanged.
s0112.idiomatic: When Di was beaten and fled, Zhaoda was recalled as protector general and given a troupe of martial music; he was re-enfeoffed as marquis of Shaowu county with two thousand households in all, keeping his regular attendant rank.

s0113.literal: In the fourth year Chen Baoying took Zhou Di in and together they raided Linchuan again; Zhaoda was again made area commander to campaign against Di.
s0113.idiomatic: In year four Chen Baoying sheltered Zhou Di and they raided Linchuan again; Zhaoda was again made area commander against Di.

s0114.literal: When he reached Dongxing Ridge, Di again withdrew and fled.
s0114.idiomatic: At Dongxing Ridge, Di again withdrew and fled.

s0115.literal: Zhaoda then crossed the ranges, halted at Jian'an, and campaigned against Chen Baoying.
s0115.idiomatic: Zhaoda then crossed the mountains, camped at Jian'an, and marched against Chen Baoying.

s0116.literal: Baoying held the border between Jian'an and Jin'an commanderies, building stockades on land and water to resist the imperial army.
s0116.idiomatic: Baoying held the border of Jian'an and Jin'an commanderies with stockades on land and water against the imperial army.

s0117.literal: Zhaoda fought without success; he therefore held the upper reaches of the river, ordered the soldiers to cut trees with branches and leaves to make rafts, mounted pounders on them, linked them with great ropes, and set camps in succession lining both banks.
s0117.idiomatic: Zhaoda fought without success, then held the upper river, had his men cut trees with branches for rafts, mounted pounders on them, linked them with great ropes, and lined camps along both banks.

s0118.literal: Baoying repeatedly offered battle; Zhaoda kept his armor on and did not move.
s0118.idiomatic: Baoying repeatedly challenged him to battle; Zhaoda held his troops still.

s0119.literal: Before long a violent rainstorm came; the river rose greatly; Zhaoda released the rafts to crash into Baoying's water stockades, and the water stockades were all broken.
s0119.idiomatic: Soon a violent storm swelled the river; Zhaoda sent the rafts to smash Baoying's water stockades and broke them all.

s0120.literal: He also sent troops out to attack Baoying's infantry.
s0120.idiomatic: He also sent troops to attack Baoying's infantry.

s0121.literal: Just as the great battle was joining, Emperor Wen sent Yu Xiaoqing out by the sea route.
s0121.idiomatic: As the great battle was joining, Emperor Wen sent Yu Xiaoqing by sea.

s0122.literal: He arrived at the right moment; they therefore joined forces and pressed the attack; Baoying was routed in great disorder; they thereupon pacified Minzhong, capturing Liu Yi, Baoying, and the rest.
s0122.idiomatic: He arrived in time; together they pressed the attack; Baoying was routed; they pacified Minzhong and seized Liu Yi, Baoying, and the rest.

s0123.literal: For merit he was appointed general who guards the van and opener of the mansion equal to the three dukes.
s0123.idiomatic: For merit he was made general who guards the van and opener of the mansion equal to the three dukes.

s0124.literal: Earlier Emperor Wen had once dreamed that Zhaoda ascended a platform beam; at dawn he told him the dream.
s0124.idiomatic: Earlier Emperor Wen had dreamed that Zhaoda climbed a platform beam; at dawn he told him the dream.

s0125.literal: On this occasion, while attending a banquet, Emperor Wen turned to Zhaoda and said, "Do you remember the dream?
s0125.idiomatic: At a banquet Emperor Wen turned to Zhaoda and said, "Do you remember the dream?

s0126.literal: How will you repay the dream?

s0127.literal: " Zhaoda replied, "I shall exert myself like a dog or horse to fulfill my minister's duty; beyond that I have nothing with which to repay you.
s0127.idiomatic: " Zhaoda answered, "I shall serve like a dog or horse and fulfill my duty as a minister; beyond that I have nothing to offer in repayment.

s0128.literal: " Soon he was again sent out as bearer of the staff, area commander over military affairs in the three prefectures of Jiang, E, and Wu, general who garrisons the south, and inspector of Jiang prefecture; his regular attendant status, opener of the mansion equal to the three dukes, and martial music were unchanged.
s0128.idiomatic: " Soon he was sent out again as bearer of the staff, commander of armies in Jiang, E, and Wu prefectures, general who garrisons the south, and inspector of Jiang prefecture, with his regular attendant rank, mansion equal to the three dukes, and martial music unchanged.

s0129.literal: When the Deposed Emperor took the throne, [Zhaoda] was transferred to palace attendant and general who campaigns south, and re-enfeoffed as Duke of Shaoling commandery.
s0129.idiomatic: When the Deposed Emperor succeeded, Zhaoda became palace attendant and general who campaigns south and was re-enfeoffed as duke of Shaoling commandery.

s0130.literal: When Hua Jiao rebelled, his letters and proclamations all borrowed Zhaoda's name as their pretext, and he repeatedly sent envoys to win him over; Zhaoda seized all his envoys and sent them to the capital.
s0130.idiomatic: When Hua Jiao rebelled, his manifestos all invoked Zhaoda's name, and he repeatedly sent envoys to win him over; Zhaoda seized every envoy and sent them to the capital.

s0131.literal: When Jiao was pacified, [Zhaoda's] title was advanced to grand general who campaigns south, and his fief was increased to two thousand five hundred households in all.
s0131.idiomatic: When Jiao was suppressed, Zhaoda was promoted to grand general who campaigns south, with his fief raised to two thousand five hundred households in all.

s0132.literal: When his term expired, he was summoned as grand general who pacifies the center; his palace attendant status, opener of the mansion equal to the three dukes, and martial music were unchanged.
s0132.idiomatic: When his term expired he was recalled as grand general who pacifies the center, keeping his palace attendant rank, mansion equal to the three dukes, and martial music.

s0133.literal: When Emperor Xuan took the throne, [Zhaoda's] title was advanced to grand general of chariots and cavalry; because his return to court was delayed, the responsible offices impeached him, and his title was reduced to general of chariots and cavalry.
s0133.idiomatic: When Emperor Xuan succeeded, Zhaoda was promoted to grand general of chariots and cavalry; because he lingered on the road, the responsible offices impeached him and his title was reduced to general of chariots and cavalry.

s0134.literal: Ouyang He held the land south of the ranges in rebellion; an edict ordered Zhaoda to take overall command of the armies to campaign against him.
s0134.idiomatic: Ouyang He rebelled in possession of the far south; an edict put Zhaoda in overall command of the armies against him.

s0135.literal: Zhaoda traveled day and night by double stages and reached Shixing.
s0135.idiomatic: Zhaoda marched day and night by forced stages and reached Shixing.

s0136.literal: He, hearing that Zhaoda had suddenly arrived, was alarmed and distraught and did not know what to do; he therefore came out and encamped at Kuikou, gathering much sand and stone, packing it in bamboo cages and placing it outside the water stockade to block the warships.
s0136.idiomatic: Hearing that Zhaoda had come upon him suddenly, He was alarmed and distraught; he came out and encamped at Kuikou, heaping sand and stone into bamboo cages outside the water stockade to block the fleet.

s0137.literal: Zhaoda held the upper reaches, fitted out tower ships and built pounders, and pressed the rebel stockade.
s0137.idiomatic: Zhaoda held the upper river, fitted out tower ships and built pounders, and pressed He's stockade.

s0138.literal: He also ordered the soldiers to hold blades in their mouths, go secretly through the water, and chop the bamboo cages; the cage bindings all came loose.
s0138.idiomatic: He also ordered his men to take blades in their mouths, slip through the water, and chop the bamboo cages until the bindings gave way.

s0139.literal: He then sent great ships downstream in a rush attack; the rebel masses were routed in great disorder; he thereupon captured He and sent him to the capital; Guangzhou was pacified.
s0139.idiomatic: He then sent great ships downstream in a rush attack; the rebels were routed; he seized He and sent him to the capital, and Guangzhou was pacified.

s0140.literal: For merit he was advanced to grand general of chariots and cavalry and transferred to minister of works; the rest was unchanged.
s0140.idiomatic: For merit he was promoted to grand general of chariots and cavalry and made minister of works; the rest of his honors stood.

s0141.literal: In the second year of Taijian he led an army to campaign against Xiao Kui at Jiangling.
s0141.idiomatic: In Taijian year two he led an army against Xiao Kui at Jiangling.

s0142.literal: At that time Kui and the Zhou army had stored many ships in great numbers in the Qingni channel; Zhaoda separately sent the subordinate generals Qian Daozhi, Cheng Wenji, and others in light boats to strike them and burn the ships.
s0142.idiomatic: Kui and the Northern Zhou forces had massed many ships in the Qingni channel; Zhaoda detached Qian Daozhi, Cheng Wenji, and others in light craft to strike and burn the fleet.

s0143.literal: The Zhou troops also built a fort on the south bank below the gorge; Editorial footnote marker 6. it was named Anshu City; they stretched a great rope across the river and wove rushes into a bridge; Editorial footnote marker 7. to convey army grain.
s0143.idiomatic: The Zhou troops also built a fort on the south bank below the gorge [6] called Anshu City, stretched a great rope across the river, and wove rushes into a bridge [7] to move army grain.

s0144.literal: Zhaoda thereupon ordered the soldiers to make long halberds, mount them on tower ships, and cut the rope from below; when the rope was severed the grain supply was cut off; he then sent the troops out to attack the fort and it surrendered.
s0144.idiomatic: Zhaoda had his men make long halberds on tower ships and cut the rope from below; when it parted the grain supply failed; he then attacked the fort and it surrendered.

s0145.literal: In the third year he fell ill and died, aged fifty-four.
s0145.idiomatic: In year three he fell ill and died at fifty-four.

s0146.literal: Posthumously he was awarded the title of grand general, his fief was increased by five hundred households, and twenty ceremonial swords were granted.
s0146.idiomatic: Posthumously he was made grand general, given five hundred added households, and granted twenty ceremonial swords.

s0147.literal: Zhaoda's nature was stern and harsh; whenever he received orders to campaign he always traveled day and night by double stages;
s0147.idiomatic: Zhaoda was stern and harsh; whenever he took the field he marched day and night by forced stages;

s0148.literal: yet whenever he won a victory he always pushed the merit onto his generals; kitchen fare and drink were the same as those of the rank and file, and the officers and soldiers for this reason attached themselves to him.
s0148.idiomatic: yet whenever he won he pushed the credit to his generals, ate and drank as his men did, and the troops for that reason gave him their loyalty.

s0149.literal: At every drinking gathering he always set out female performers and mixed music to the full, with every sound of the Qiang and Hu, melody and bearing all the finest of the age; even when facing the enemy with banners and drums confronting one another, he did not abandon it.
s0149.idiomatic: At every feast he set out female performers and every sort of music, Qiang and Hu sounds, melody and bearing the finest of the age; even with enemy banners and drums in sight he would not give it up.

s0150.literal: In the fourth year he was granted shared offerings in Emperor Wen's temple hall.
s0150.idiomatic: In year four he was granted shared offerings in Emperor Wen's temple.

s0151.literal: His son Dabao inherited the enfeoffment as Duke of Shaoling commandery and rose through offices to scattered-cavalry regular attendant and protector general.
s0151.idiomatic: His son Dabao inherited the dukedom of Shaoling commandery and rose to scattered-cavalry regular attendant and protector general.

s0152.literal: Sent out as inspector of Feng prefecture, in the prefecture he was greedy and unrestrained; the common people resented him bitterly; the Later Lord replaced him with the grand master of the imperial stud Li Yun.
s0152.idiomatic: Sent out as inspector of Feng prefecture, he ruled with greed and license until the people bitterly resented him; the Later Lord replaced him with Li Yun, grand master of the imperial stud.

s0153.literal: In the fourth month of the third year of Zhide, as Yun was about to reach the prefecture, Dabao suddenly attacked and killed Yun, raised troops in rebellion, and sent his general Yang Tong to raid Jian'an.
s0153.idiomatic: In the fourth month of Zhide year three, as Yun was nearing the prefecture, Dabao ambushed and killed him, rebelled, and sent his general Yang Tong against Jian'an.

s0154.literal: Wu Huijue, interior secretary of Jian'an, held the commandery city in resistance; Tong repeatedly attacked but could not take it.
s0154.idiomatic: Wu Huijue, interior secretary of Jian'an, held the commandery city; Tong attacked again and again but could not take it.

s0155.literal: As the imperial army drew nearer, hearts turned away from him; Dabao's plans were exhausted; he and Tong both fled.
s0155.idiomatic: As the imperial army drew near, loyalty fell away; Dabao was at his wits' end and fled with Tong.

s0156.literal: Chen Jingxiang, commander of the capital army, led troops in pursuit of Dabao.
s0156.idiomatic: Chen Jingxiang, commander of the capital army, pursued Dabao.

s0157.literal: Once Dabao had entered the mountains, the mountain roads were rugged and steep and he could go no farther; Tong carried him on his back and advanced little by little.
s0157.idiomatic: Once in the mountains the paths were too steep for Dabao to walk; Tong carried him on his back and moved on step by step.

s0158.literal: Before long the pursuers overtook them; he was captured alive and sent to the capital; he died on the road; his head was transmitted and displayed at the Vermilion Bird Bridge; three generations of his clan were exterminated.
s0158.idiomatic: Soon the pursuers caught them; Dabao was taken alive and sent to the capital but died on the road; his head was displayed at the Vermilion Bird Bridge, and three generations of his clan were exterminated.

s0159.literal: The historiographer says: Huang Faqu and Chunyu Liang, meeting the disorders at the end of Liang when Liu and Xiang had not yet been decided, were among the very few who could distinguish light from dark and see right from wrong; the two lords understood the principle of which side to follow and rose to the chief minister's tripod—this too was their wisdom.
s0159.idiomatic: The historiographer writes: Huang Faqu and Chunyu Liang lived through the chaos at the end of Liang, when the realm had not yet chosen between rival founders; men who could tell right from wrong were few. Both understood which side to take and rose to the highest offices—that was their wisdom.

s0160.literal: Zhaoda and Emperor Wen were old friends from the same native place; their bond was like that of Deng and Xiao; when Emperor Wen took the succession he entrusted Zhaoda with weighty responsibility; as for victory in battle and success in attack, repeatedly pacifying rebellions—he too was a worthy minister and worthy general, a Wu and Geng of his generation.
s0160.idiomatic: Zhaoda and Emperor Wen were old friends from the same country; their bond was like that of Deng Yu and Xiao He. When Wen took the throne he gave Zhaoda great trust; in battle and siege he again and again crushed rebellion—a worthy minister and general, a Wu Han and Geng Yan for his age.

s0162.literal: Qi sent its Prince of Liyang with fifty thousand foot and horse to relieve them—comment:
s0162.idiomatic: On "Qi sent its Prince of Liyang with fifty thousand foot and horse to relieve them":

s0164.literal: says "Qi sent one hundred thousand troops to relieve Liyang," while this says "fifty thousand," differing from the annals.
s0164.idiomatic: reads "Qi sent one hundred thousand troops to relieve Liyang," while this reads fifty thousand, differing from the annals.

s0165.literal: Summoned as grand general who pacifies the center—"grand general who pacifies the center"
s0165.idiomatic: On "summoned as grand general who pacifies the center":

s0167.literal: reads "grand general who pacifies the army," and the History of the Southern Dynasties also reads "grand general who pacifies the army."
s0167.idiomatic: reads grand general who pacifies the army, and the History of the Southern Dynasties also reads grand general who pacifies the army.

s0168.literal: Comment: in various books "pacifies the center" is sometimes written "pacifies the army."
s0168.idiomatic: Note: in various books pacifies the center is sometimes written pacifies the army.

s0169.literal: Many longed for their native soil—"soil" was originally corrupt as "born"; other editions are not corrupt; now corrected.
s0169.idiomatic: On "many longed for their native soil": soil was originally written born; other editions are correct; emended.

s0170.literal: Summoned as grand general who guards the center—"grand general who guards the center"
s0170.idiomatic: On "summoned as grand general who guards the center":

s0172.literal: in Taijian years five and six both read "grand general of the central guard," and the biography of Xu Ling reads "general of the central guard."
s0172.idiomatic: in Taijian years five and six both read grand general of the central guard, and the biography of Xu Ling reads general of the central guard.

s0173.literal: Soon he followed Hou Andu and others in resisting Wang Lin at
s0173.idiomatic: Soon he followed Hou Andu and others in resisting Wang Lin at

s0180.literal: Comment: Hu's note to the Comprehensive Mirror says, "Zhakou lies east of Ruru Ford; water leads to Chaohu Lake and is now called Zhakou River."
s0180.idiomatic: Note: Hu's commentary to the Comprehensive Mirror says Zhakou lies east of Ruru Ford; its waters lead to Chaohu and it is now called Zhakou River.

s0181.literal: If it were Chun Ford, that would be where Wang Lin earlier inflicted a great defeat on the Chen army and Hou Andu and others were captured—at the mouth where Chun River enters the Yangzi, far west of Zhakou.
s0181.idiomatic: If it were Chun Ford, that would be where Wang Lin earlier routed the Chen army and captured Hou Andu and others—at the mouth where the Chun River enters the Yangzi, far west of Zhakou.

s0182.literal: The Zhou troops also built a fort on the south bank below the gorge—"below the gorge" in the History of the Southern Dynasties reads "gorge mouth," the Comprehensive Mirror the same.
s0182.idiomatic: On "the Zhou troops also built a fort on the south bank below the gorge": the History of the Southern Dynasties reads gorge mouth, the Comprehensive Mirror the same.

s0183.literal: Comment: Hu's note to the Comprehensive Mirror says: "Gorge mouth is the mouth of Xiling Gorge."
s0183.idiomatic: Note: Hu's commentary to the Comprehensive Mirror says gorge mouth is the mouth of Xiling Gorge.

s0184.literal: Binding rush mats into a bridge—the graph wei (rush mat) in the Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Palace editions all read wei (reed); the History of the Southern Dynasties and Comprehensive Mirror agree.
s0184.idiomatic: On "binding rush into a bridge": the graph wei (rush mat) in the Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Palace editions all read wei (reed); the History of the Southern Dynasties and Comprehensive Mirror agree.
